title: The sailing dahabiya
standfirst: A dahabiya is the Nile’s traditional sailing houseboat: a small group, a shaded deck and nights at quiet moorings away from the town quays. This is one of the vessel types in our guide to [[up]].

sections.heading: What a dahabiya is
paragraphs: Dahabiyas are flat-bottomed sailing boats with two masts and large triangular sails. They were the way wealthy travellers saw Egypt in the nineteenth century, and the modern ones follow the same design with en-suite cabins and an open upper deck.
They sail when there is wind. When there isn’t, a small tug or motor launch tows them, so the timetable still holds.

sections.heading: Life on board
paragraphs: With only a handful of cabins, a dahabiya feels like a private house. Meals are often served at one table, the crew is small, and there is room on deck for everyone at once. There is usually no pool, no evening show and no crowd at the gangway.

sections.heading: Where dahabiyas sail
paragraphs: Most dahabiya cruises sail between Esna and Aswan over four or five nights. Because they moor at riverbanks and islands, they can stop at sites the big ships pass by, and the evenings are quiet.

sections.heading: Is a dahabiya for you?
paragraphs: Choose a dahabiya for a small group, a slower pace and flexibility. Choose a cruise ship if you want a pool, a gym or a lower starting price. Prices for dahabiyas vary widely: the size of the cabin, the crew per guest and the season matter more than the label.

faqs.q: How many guests does a dahabiya take?
faqs.a: Usually a dozen to about twenty, in six to ten cabins. Each vessel’s page shows its own figure.
Only when the wind allows. Otherwise a tug tows it, so the planned stops and times are kept.
